content: The safety and efficacy of YAZ were evaluated over a one-year period in a study involving 1,027 women aged 17 to 36 who received at least one dose of the medication. A second Phase 3 study was conducted as a single-center, open-label, active-controlled trial to assess the effects of seven 28-day cycles of YAZ on carbohydrate metabolism, lipid profiles, and hemostasis in 29 women aged 18 to 35. For acne treatment, two multicenter, double-blind, randomized, placebo-controlled studies were conducted in 536 women aged 14 to 45 with moderate acne vulgaris. These studies evaluated the safety and efficacy of YAZ over six cycles in participants who received at least one dose of the medication. For folate supplementation, a primary efficacy study was conducted using drospirenone/ethinyl estradiol/levomefolate calcium and levomefolate calcium. This multicenter, double-blind, randomized, active-controlled U.S. trial involved 379 healthy women aged 18 to 40 who were treated with either drospirenone/ethinyl estradiol/levomefolate calcium, levomefolate calcium, or YAZ for up to 24 weeks. Adverse reactions observed across the three indications (contraception, acne, and folate supplementation) overlapped and were reported using pooled data frequencies. No adverse reaction leading to discontinuation occurred in ≥1% of women. For PMDD (premenstrual dysphoric disorder), safety data from clinical trials were reported separately due to differences in study design and settings compared to the contraception, acne, and folate supplementation studies. Two multicenter, double-blind, randomized, placebo-controlled trials (one parallel and one crossover design) evaluated the safety and efficacy of YAZ for treating PMDD symptoms over three cycles in 285 women aged 18 to 42 who were diagnosed with PMDD and received at least one dose of the medication. Serious adverse reactions reported in clinical trials included the following: For contraception trials: None reported. For folate supplementation trials: Cervical carcinoma stage 0. For PMDD trials: Cervical dysplasia. Postmarketing experience identified additional adverse reactions, which were reported voluntarily and are grouped by System Organ Classes. These include: Vascular disorders: Venous and arterial thromboembolic events (e.g., pulmonary embolism, deep vein thrombosis, cerebral thrombosis, retinal thrombosis, myocardial infarction, stroke), and hypertension (including hypertensive crisis). Hepatobiliary disorders: Gallbladder disease, liver function disturbances, and liver tumors. Immune system disorders: Hypersensitivity reactions, including anaphylaxis. Metabolism and nutrition disorders: Hyperkalemia, hypertriglyceridemia, changes in glucose tolerance, and effects on peripheral insulin resistance (including diabetes mellitus). Skin and subcutaneous tissue disorders: Chloasma, angioedema, erythema nodosum, and erythema multiforme. Gastrointestinal disorders: Inflammatory bowel disease. Musculoskeletal and connective tissue disorders: Systemic lupus erythematosus. Drug interactions with YAZ and other combined oral contraceptives (COCs) were also noted: Substances that diminish the efficacy of COCs include drugs or herbal products that induce certain enzymes, such as CYP3A4. Examples include phenytoin, barbiturates, carbamazepine, bosentan, felbamate, griseofulvin, oxcarbazepine, rifampicin, topiramate, and St. John’s wort. These interactions may lead to breakthrough bleeding or contraceptive failure. Women should be counseled to use alternative or backup contraception during and for 28 days after discontinuing enzyme inducers. Substances that increase plasma concentrations of COCs include atorvastatin, ascorbic acid, acetaminophen, and CYP3A4 inhibitors (e.g., itraconazole, ketoconazole). These may increase plasma hormone levels, potentially altering the drug's effects.
